claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by formation and stability of a self-limiting passivating oxide shell.
Cr-, Al-, or similarly oxyphilic alloying elements can form compact, self-healing protective oxide layers such as Cr2O3 or Al2O3.
A passivating oxide shell suppresses atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
A passivating oxide shell suppresses phase segregation in near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
High-entropy alloys can maintain random solid-solution structures without forming intermetallic compounds at operating temperatures because of high configurational entropy.
An oxidizing atmosphere promotes formation and retention of the proposed passivating oxide layer.
At high operating temperatures, oxyphilic alloy components preferentially oxidize into a self-healing, compact oxide coating.
The oxide coating acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
The oxide coating inhibits surface segregation and nanoparticle coarsening.
Inhibiting segregation and coarsening preserves the nanoparticle solid-solution structure and catalytic or thermoelectric functionality.
Nanoparticles lacking the oxide-forming element have fewer barriers to high-temperature elemental migration and phase separation.

Nanoparticles containing an oxide-forming element such as Cr will be more structurally and chemically stable under high-temperature oxidizing conditions than otherwise comparable nanoparticles depleted of that element.
The Cr-containing nanoparticles will resist coarsening, elemental segregation, coalescence, and secondary-phase formation relative to Cr-depleted nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is primarily applicable in oxidizing or mildly oxidative environments and may fail in reducing environments because the oxide layer is compromised.
The cited catalytic and thermoelectric temperature ranges are representative service conditions for the proposed nanoparticle comparison.
